                                                                                      Agentic Build Lab

                                                                                      How this lab works · 5 minutes to read

                                                                                      In one day you'll build a ServiceNow app called the HR Case Router. It's based on a real use case from your company.

                                                                                      When a new HR case comes in, an AI agent moves it to the assignment group or HR service that should work it. It adds a work note that says why it chose that one. If it can't route a case, or a safety check stops the move, the case stays where it is. The work note says why. All of this happens on its own, as soon as the case is created. If a fulfiller, someone who works HR cases, thinks a case is in the wrong place, they can click Reroute. The agent then routes it again, the same way.

                                                                                      You tell Claude Code how the app should work and which checks it must pass. Claude Code writes the code.

                                                                                      What you learn is a way to build with AI that you can trust:

                                                                                      • Catch mistakes early, before any code exists.
                                                                                      • Agree on a design before anything is built.
                                                                                      • Let checks decide whether work moves on, not anyone's say-so.
                                                                                      • Trust evidence you can run again, such as a command's output, over Claude's summary of it.
                                                                                      • Write down decisions and progress, so someone else could pick up the work.

                                                                                      Each time the process stops a real mistake, that's a catch. You'll count yours at the end of the day.

                                                                                      A PRD is a product requirements document: what the app must do. An LLD is a low-level design: how the app will do it.

                                                                                      From 16:20 to 17:00 there's time to catch up. If you fall behind, ask your instructor for a checkpoint. A checkpoint is the work so far, ready made, so you can start the next module from it.

                                                                                      You can read this guide as one page once you've done step 4 of the pre-work. On Mac: run this in a terminal: open ~/projects/hr-case-router-lab-guide/LAB.html. On Windows: open File Explorer and click its address bar. Type %USERPROFILE%\projects\hr-case-router-lab-guide\LAB.html and press Enter. Then open Setup, the first button in the top bar, and click Copy my setup. That brings your answers across.

                                                                                      You work alone on the day. Your partner joins you after the workshop. They attack your app and test your runbook, the steps for running and fixing it.

                                                                                      What you need

                                                                                      You need Details
                                                                                      A ServiceNow instance An instance is your own ServiceNow site. Your instructor gives you one. It has HR Service Delivery, its demo data and AI Agent Studio, and you're an admin on it. Never use a production instance, the one real people use.
                                                                                      A computer you can install software on On Mac: macOS 13 or later. On Windows: only by arrangement with your instructor, for now. You use WSL, which runs Linux inside Windows, or Git Bash, a Linux-style terminal. The pre-work's Windows steps are still being tested. Linux works too. If your company laptop blocks installs, tell your instructor two weeks before.
                                                                                      A Claude plan that includes Claude Code Max, Team, Enterprise and a Claude Console account all work. Pro works too, but it runs one sub-agent at a time. A sub-agent is a helper Claude starts for part of the work. Module 6 shows how to work with one. The free plan doesn't include Claude Code. On Pro or Max, first turn off model training in claude.ai Settings > Privacy.
                                                                                      A GitHub account A personal account is simplest. A company account works only if it can create private repos. The lab needs GitHub. Your company's GitLab can't stand in for it. Send your instructor your user name by the pre-session, a week before. Then accept their invite to this guide.
                                                                                      About 2 hours, at least two days before That's for the pre-work. If you can, also come to the pre-session a week before. It takes an hour.

                                                                                      Claude Code, in the terminal. This guide is written for Claude Code in a terminal window.

                                                                                      Claude Code, in the Code tab. Where the desktop app works differently, the guide shows its way. You still need a terminal app and the claude command for the ⌨️ steps. Those are installing the kit, the checks, and every password.

                                                                                      The pre-work installs everything else. That includes the prove-it kit, the Claude Code plugin the lab runs on. A plugin is an add-on for Claude Code.

                                                                                      What you should be able to do

                                                                                      Before the day, you should be able to:

                                                                                      1. Log in to a ServiceNow instance as an admin. Open a list, such as the HR cases. Impersonate a user, which means acting as them, when you're given the menu path.
                                                                                      2. Open a terminal. Paste a command into it, run it, and read what it prints.
                                                                                      3. Start Claude Code and send it a message. Answer it when it asks permission to run a command.
                                                                                      4. Say in one sentence each what a repo, a commit and a pull request are.
                                                                                      5. Install software on your computer, or get it installed in time.

                                                                                      You don't need to write code or know git's commands. Git is the tool that keeps a project's history. You don't need to have used the ServiceNow SDK either. The SDK is the toolkit for building ServiceNow apps on your own computer. Claude writes the code and runs git. You read and decide.

                                                                                      New to any of these? That's normal. Most people are new to at least one. Two things help:

                                                                                      • Come to the pre-session a week before. It shows items 2 and 3 live and answers your questions.
                                                                                      • Set Detail level to Explain more, in the top bar. Help boxes open, and the guide explains its words where you first meet them. You can change it at any time.

                                                                                      Where you act

                                                                                      Every action starts with one of these labels.

                                                                                      Label What you do
                                                                                      🤖 Claude Type it into Claude Code
                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal Type it into a normal terminal, never into Claude
                                                                                      ✏️ Editor Open or change the file yourself, in VS Code
                                                                                      🌐 Browser Use GitHub, or your instance as admin unless a step says to impersonate hr.demo

                                                                                      Some checks have a closed 🛟 box under them. Open it only if you see something different. ℹ️ boxes explain why, if you want to know. Detail level, in the top bar, shows more help or less, at any time.

                                                                                      On Mac, in the terminal: While Claude runs in a Terminal window, that window is Claude's. Do ⌨️ Terminal steps in a second window, your window. To open it, press Cmd+N.

                                                                                      On Windows, in the terminal: While Claude runs in a Git Bash tab, that tab is Claude's. Do ⌨️ Terminal steps in a second Git Bash tab, your window. To open it, press Ctrl+Shift+T in Windows Terminal.

                                                                                      On Mac, in the Code tab: Claude runs in the desktop app. For ⌨️ Terminal steps, your window is a window of the Terminal app. Don't use the Code tab's own terminal pane. Nobody has checked yet whether Claude can read what you type there, and passwords must stay out of Claude.

                                                                                      On Windows, in the Code tab: Claude runs in the desktop app. For ⌨️ Terminal steps, your window is a Git Bash tab in Windows Terminal. Don't use the Code tab's own terminal pane. Nobody has checked yet whether Claude can read what you type there, and passwords must stay out of Claude.

                                                                                      Typing to Claude. Claude Code has one box at the bottom, where you type. Enter sends what's in it. To start a new line without sending, type \ and then press Enter. Three kinds of thing go in that box:

                                                                                      • A 🤖 box from this guide. Sending: paste a 🤖 box, type go after it, press Enter.
                                                                                      • A line starting with /. It isn't a question for Claude. It starts something ready-made. Some are Claude Code's own commands. For example, /status shows which version you have. Others start a skill: instructions written in advance, which Claude follows step by step. Skills come with a plugin. The kit's skills all start with /prove-it:, such as /prove-it:consult in Module 2. Type / and a list appears. Keep typing to narrow it, then press Enter.
                                                                                      • A short reply. When Claude asks you something, answer in a word or two. For example, it may ask whether to keep a line.

                                                                                      Type these on their own, with no go: a line starting with /, and short replies such as yes, keep, approve, apply and ship it. Some replies must be exact, such as Confirmed.. Each step gives you the words. Copy them as shown, full stop included.

                                                                                      In the terminal: When Claude runs a command, Claude Code shows it on a line starting with ⏺. The command's output is under it, on lines starting with ⎿. Read that output, not Claude's summary. If it says … +N lines, press Ctrl+O to see it all.

                                                                                      In the Code tab: Set the view to Verbose in each new session. Open the session menu, the caret beside the session title. Choose Transcript view, then Verbose. Or press Ctrl+O until it shows. The normal view folds each command into a summary. Verbose shows every tool call, which means each thing Claude runs. Read what each command printed, not Claude's summary.

                                                                                      🛟 Claude closed, or the window crashed, mid-step?

                                                                                      In the terminal: Go to the same folder and run claude --continue. It reopens the conversation where it stopped.

                                                                                      In the Code tab: Open the desktop app again and click the session in the sidebar. The session still holds the conversation.

                                                                                      Rules for the whole lab

                                                                                      1. Never paste this guide into Claude. Only the text in 🤖 boxes goes in. Why: if Claude sees the checks, it can write work that just passes them. Then they stop being checks.
                                                                                      2. Passwords stay out of Claude. Type them only into your own terminal or your browser. Claude never runs now-sdk auth, the command that asks for your instance's password. Why: everything you type into Claude is sent to the AI model. It also stays in the conversation's history.
                                                                                      3. You decide when your instance changes. You install the app yourself. Claude runs only one install: the grade's, in Module 7, to lab-pdi, your instance's short name. It asks you first. Why: an install changes a live system. As in real work, a person decides when.
                                                                                      4. Never use a production instance. Why: the agent you build moves HR cases and writes notes on them. On production, those are real people's cases.
                                                                                      5. Trust what a command prints, not what Claude says about it. Why: Claude's summary is its best guess, and it can be wrong. The output is evidence. You can check it, or run the command again.
                                                                                      6. Follow what really happens. Don't re-run a prompt to get a nicer answer. Write down what happened, and carry on. Why: Claude can answer differently each time. Re-running until it looks right hides the mistakes the lab is built to catch.
                                                                                      ℹ️ Where a password does go

                                                                                      Your instance's password goes in two places. One is its login page, in the browser. The other is now-sdk auth, which you run in your own terminal window. You first do that in pre-work step 7. On Mac: sudo asks for admin rights. If it asks for your Mac's password, type it in your own terminal window too. The lab's settings block now-sdk auth for Claude, so Claude can't run it by mistake.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Two installs, two ways

                                                                                      In Module 6 you run now-sdk install --auth lab-pdi yourself, in your own terminal window. The grade runs in Module 7, and again after the workshop. It runs the install after asking you. That's the one install Claude runs. The lab's settings make Claude ask before any SDK command that writes to your instance, such as now-sdk install.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Behind? Don't re-run: ask

                                                                                      If a step really went wrong, or you're behind, ask your instructor for a checkpoint. You start the next module from it. That keeps a true record of what happened, and keeps you moving.

                                                                                      When Claude asks permission

                                                                                      In auto mode, the lab's default, a safety check decides for Claude. Claude rarely asks you. It blocks risky commands instead, and shows Denied by auto mode classifier. Did it block the step's own action? Reply yes, and the action, such as yes, push the branch. If not, reply no, stop.

                                                                                      When it does ask, read the command. Then find it in the table below. If two rows match, No wins. The one exception is the grade's own install to lab-pdi, which has its own row.

                                                                                      What to answer when Claude asks permission
                                                                                      The command Answer Why
                                                                                      git … or gh … Yes Your repo and your GitHub: commits, branches, issues and pull requests
                                                                                      npm … or node …, except npm run deploy Yes Installs, builds and tests on your computer
                                                                                      now-sdk build, now-sdk explain or now-sdk query --auth lab-pdi, or their npx @servicenow/sdk … forms Yes build runs on your computer. explain reads the SDK's docs. query reads your instance and changes nothing
                                                                                      Reading or changing files in ~/projects/hr-case-router, Module 1's ~/projects/hr-case-router-prd-review or the kit's copy, ~/projects/prove-it-kit Yes Claude's workspace
                                                                                      now-sdk auth No It takes your password (rule 2)
                                                                                      now-sdk install, deploy, exec, execute, run, move or cicd, in any form, or npm run deploy No They change your instance, and you decide when (rule 3)
                                                                                      The grade asks to run now-sdk install --auth lab-pdi (Module 7, and the grades after the workshop) Yes, for that command only The one install Claude runs, after asking
                                                                                      Any alias but lab-pdi, or anything that names your instance No It could reach another instance
                                                                                      Anything in this guide's folder No Claude never reads this guide (rule 1)
                                                                                      Anything else, or you're not sure No, then ask Claude what it was for A No costs a minute. A wrong Yes may not be undone
                                                                                      • Never choose "Yes, and don't ask again". The asking is the check.
                                                                                      • Asked "Allow this read outside the working directories?" This comes once. Choose Yes, and keep allowing any reads outside the working directories. It's safe: the lab's settings still keep Claude out of this guide, your notes and your keys.

                                                                                      Words you'll meet

                                                                                      • Repo: a folder whose history git keeps. Your app's repo is ~/projects/hr-case-router/app.
                                                                                      • Commit: one saved snapshot in a repo's history.
                                                                                      • Branch: a separate line of commits. Work happens on a branch, so main, the repo's main line, changes only through pull requests.
                                                                                      • Pull request: a request on GitHub to merge a branch into main. It's reviewed before it merges.
                                                                                      • Story: one small piece of work, filed as a GitHub issue. An issue is a to-do item on GitHub.
                                                                                      • Gate: a milestone that waits for its stories to finish. There are four: MERGE, INSTALL, DEMO and HANDOFF.
                                                                                      • Design term: one numbered rule in your design record, such as C3. Every test names the term it proves.
                                                                                      • Catch: a real problem the process found and that got fixed, or that changed a decision. If you plant a problem to test a check, the check firing on it isn't a catch.

                                                                                      Claude also writes short labels, such as C3, P8 or §7. The appendix says what each one means. Each step that uses one also has an ℹ️ box.

                                                                                      Your folders and your catches

                                                                                      After the pre-work, your ~/projects folder holds:

                                                                                      hr-case-router-lab-guide/   this guide: you read it, Claude never does
hr-case-router/             your workspace: Claude works here
  app/                      your app's repo, private on GitHub
  brief/                    the PRD, from Module 1
  catches.md                one line per catch
hr-case-router-notes/       what Module 8 restores: Claude never reads it
prove-it-kit/               a copy of the kit

                                                                                      You don't write notes yourself. At the end of each module, a Log it prompt has Claude draft that module's catches, one line each. Reply keep, or say what to change:

                                                                                      <module> | <what caught it> | <what it caught, and what was done>

                                                                                      For example: 1 | prd | An input asked for something the PRD left out; I listed it under Open decisions. Module 8 counts them.

                                                                                      ℹ️ New to ServiceNow? Four moves cover every step
                                                                                      • The filter navigator is the search box at the top left. Click All to see it. Type a table name and .list, such as sn_hr_core_case.list. Press Enter to open that table as a list.
                                                                                      • To filter a list, type in the search box at the top of a column. Then press Enter.
                                                                                      • To make a record, click New on a list. Fill in the form, then click Submit.
                                                                                      • A reference field has a 🔍 beside it. It points to another record. Click the 🔍 and pick one.

                                                                                      ⏱ About 2 hours · at home, at least two days before the workshop

                                                                                      Your bench is everything you build with: your instance, your tools, Claude Code and a private repo for your app. Get it ready before the workshop. Then read the customer's inputs, the files where the customer says what they need. On the day, you start building straight away. There's nothing left to install.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why are we doing this?
                                                                                      • In real work: people set up the bench before they build. That stops mistakes from leaking out, such as secrets, stray files or the wrong instance. Secrets are passwords, keys and tokens.
                                                                                      • Why it matters: your repo takes in only the files you name. A guard, a script that runs before each commit, checks it for secrets. You set them up once, and they protect every commit after that.
                                                                                      • Your mindset: a safety check you've never seen fail is a hope, not a check. Test it before you rely on it.

                                                                                      You need the instance, the Claude plan and the GitHub account listed in the README, under What you need.

                                                                                      Send your instructor: what, and by when
                                                                                      Send your instructor By when
                                                                                      Your GitHub user name. If you have no account yet, step 4 helps you make one As soon as you can, and by the pre-session, the one-hour online session a week before. Your instructor needs it to invite you
                                                                                      "Done", or what's still missing from You now have, the list at the end of this page At least two days before the workshop
                                                                                      Anything that stops an install, such as a proxy, a certificate error or no admin rights As soon as you hit it. If you can, two weeks before the workshop

                                                                                      Part 1 — Your instance

                                                                                      1. Get your instance

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      You build the app on your own instance, and install it there. You'll need the instance's name twice. It goes into the sign-in for the SDK, ServiceNow's toolkit for building apps on your computer. It also goes into the guard that keeps the name out of your commits. So note it now.

                                                                                      Your instructor gives you your own instance, your own ServiceNow site. It comes with HR Service Delivery, ServiceNow's HR app, and its demo data. It also has AI Agent Studio, where AI agents are built. Save the instance's admin password in your password manager. Note its address, such as https://dev123456.service-now.com.

                                                                                      Note the instance's name too. It's the first part of the address, such as dev123456.

                                                                                      2. Check your instance

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      If a user, group or role is missing, checking now finds it while there's still time to fix it. That's better than finding it on the morning of the workshop.

                                                                                      Check that your instance has what the lab needs. That's the demo data, the lab's groups and users, and an ordinary HR fulfiller who can see HR cases. A fulfiller is someone who works HR cases.

                                                                                      Your instance comes with hr.demo, an HR fulfiller with no admin rights. Stay logged in as admin. When a step says so, impersonate hr.demo, which means you act as that user.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why an ordinary fulfiller?
                                                                                      • In real work: the people who click Reroute, to have a case routed again, are HR agents. They aren't admins.
                                                                                      • Why it matters: admin passes every access check. So a check done as admin proves nothing. Only an ordinary fulfiller shows whether the app's role, the HR access rules and the agent work for the people who'll use them. Every live check in this lab is done as hr.demo.

                                                                                      🌐 Browser: log in to your instance as admin.

                                                                                      1. Click All at the top left. Type sn_hr_core_case.list in the box under it, and press Enter. Then do the same with sn_hr_core_service.list. ✅ Both lists have rows: demo HR cases and HR services.

                                                                                      2. Open sys_user_group.list the same way. In the Name column's search box, type Lab and press Enter. ✅ It lists Lab HR Team and Lab Locked Out.

                                                                                      3. Open sys_user.list. In the User ID column's search box, type hr.router and press Enter. ✅ It's listed. The agent runs as this user, so never impersonate it or change it. Do the same for hr.demo.

                                                                                        Is hr.demo listed?

                                                                                        If it isn't listed: your instance hasn't been prepared for the lab.

                                                                                        ⛔ Stop here until your instructor has prepared your instance. Every check in this lab runs as hr.demo. Don't make the user yourself. Send your instructor this message, in the room's chat or by email:

                                                                                        Lab: my instance has no hr.demo user. Instance: <your instance's name, such as dev123456>.

                                                                                        Meanwhile, do Part 2, steps 3 to 7. It doesn't need hr.demo. Then come back here.

                                                                                        Open hr.demo.

                                                                                      4. In its Roles tab: ✅ it lists sn_hr_core.case_writer and sn_hr_le.case_writer. If one is missing, click Edit.... Move it from the left list to the right, and click Save.

                                                                                      5. In its Groups tab: ✅ it lists Lab HR Team. If it doesn't, click Edit.... Move Lab HR Team from the left list to the right, and click Save.

                                                                                      6. Impersonate hr.demo. Click your avatar at the top right of the instance, then Impersonate user. In the dialog, type hr.demo, pick HR Demo, and click Impersonate user. Close any welcome pop-up.

                                                                                      7. Open sn_hr_core_case.list. ✅ It lists HR cases.

                                                                                      8. End impersonation. Click your avatar, then End impersonation. You're admin again.

                                                                                      🛟 It's asleep or gone, or has no HR cases
                                                                                      • Asleep: Your instance is asleep. Open it in your browser. If its page offers a wake-up link, click it and wait. Waking can take up to 20 minutes. If there's no link, or it's still asleep, ask your instructor.
                                                                                      • Gone, or no HR cases: tell your instructor.
                                                                                      🛟 hr.router, hr.demo or a group is missing, or hr.demo sees no cases

                                                                                      Tell your instructor. The instance hasn't been prepared for the lab. Never make hr.router or a group yourself. Don't give hr.demo any other role, and nothing admin. Later, in Module 6, it gets the app's own role.

                                                                                      Part 2 — Your tools

                                                                                      Tools at a glance: what step 3 checks and installs, and why the lab needs each one.

                                                                                      Tools at a glance: what each tool is, why the lab needs it, and its version
                                                                                      Tool What it is Why the lab needs it Version
                                                                                      Node.js Runs JavaScript programs on your computer. It comes with npm, which installs them. The ServiceNow SDK runs on it, and npm installs the SDK. npm also installs your app's packages, the code your app builds on, and runs its tests. The lab's settings script runs on Node.js too. v22.22 or later
                                                                                      git Keeps a folder's history. Each saved snapshot is a commit. Your app's repo, its guard, and a branch for every story all use git. Claude runs most git commands. You read what they print. On Windows: Git for Windows also brings Git Bash, a Linux-style terminal. You run every ⌨️ step in it. The lab's settings, in step 5, keep Claude in it too, where the safety rules apply. Any
                                                                                      GitHub CLI (gh) GitHub's own command-line tool. You type its commands in a terminal. It signs you in to GitHub, gets this guide and makes your app's private repo. It also lets the kit, the lab's Claude Code plugin, file your stories, milestones and pull requests. Any
                                                                                      ServiceNow SDK (now-sdk) ServiceNow's tool for building an app as code, from files on your computer. It builds the HR Case Router, reads your instance and installs the app on it. 4.8.0 or later
                                                                                      Claude Code (claude) Claude, working in your folders. It reads and writes files, and runs commands. It writes the app. You make the decisions. It has its own installer and doesn't need Node.js. 2.1.228 or later
                                                                                      VS Code A free code editor. You open and check the files Claude writes in it. Those are the ✏️ steps. Any

                                                                                      Using the desktop app's Code tab? Install the claude command too. The lab's plugins and checks run from a terminal.

                                                                                      3. Install the tools

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      Every later step runs one of these tools. If one is missing or too old, it fails in ways that are hard to read. The check comes first, so you install only what's missing.

                                                                                      On Mac: open Terminal. Press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and press Enter.

                                                                                      On Windows: these Windows steps are still being tested. If a step shows something it doesn't describe, stop there. Tell your instructor what you see.

                                                                                      First, set up Git Bash, the terminal every ⌨️ step uses:

                                                                                      1. 🌐 Browser: open https://git-scm.com/downloads/win. Click Git for Windows/x64 Setup. On an ARM computer, click Git for Windows/ARM64 Setup instead.
                                                                                      2. Open the file from your Downloads folder.
                                                                                      3. Click Yes when Windows asks to allow changes.
                                                                                      4. Click Next on each screen until Select Components.
                                                                                      5. Tick Add a Git Bash Profile to Windows Terminal. Keep every other default.
                                                                                      6. Click Next on each screen that's left, then Install, then Finish.
                                                                                      7. Open Windows Terminal. Press the Windows key, type Terminal and press Enter.
                                                                                      8. Click ⌄, beside the + at the top. Then click Settings.
                                                                                      9. In Settings > Startup, set Default profile to Git Bash. Click Save.
                                                                                      10. Close every Windows Terminal window.

                                                                                      Then open Windows Terminal again. It opens in Git Bash.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Never installed tools like these? How this step goes
                                                                                      1. Run the check below, even on a new computer. command not found means that tool isn't installed yet. That's expected.
                                                                                      2. Answer No, one is missing or too old. Each tool's install then shows under the question, step by step. They're in the order to do them.
                                                                                      3. Install only the tools that failed, top to bottom.
                                                                                      4. An installer may ask for your computer's password, or for permission to make changes. That's expected. If you can't give it because your company manages the computer, tell your instructor before the day.
                                                                                      5. When you've installed them, close every terminal window. Then open a new one, and run the check again. A window that was open before an install can't see the new tool.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal: check what you have:

                                                                                      node --version
git --version
gh --version
now-sdk --version
claude --version
                                                                                      1. node --versionPrints which version of Node.js you have, such as v22.22.0. Node.js runs now-sdk, and its npm installs now-sdk. command not found means it isn't installed yet, or this window opened before you installed it.
                                                                                      2. git --versionPrints which version of git you have. git keeps a history of your files, one commit at a time. Your app's repo is a git repo.
                                                                                      3. gh --versionPrints the version of gh, GitHub's own command-line tool, then a web address. Step 4 uses it to sign in to GitHub and to download this guide.
                                                                                      4. now-sdk --versionPrints the version of ServiceNow's SDK tool, such as 4.13.6. It builds your app from the files on your computer and installs it on your instance.
                                                                                      5. claude --versionPrints the version of Claude Code, such as 2.1.312 (Claude Code). Claude Code is the coding agent you build the app with.

                                                                                      ✅ Node.js is v22.22 or later, now-sdk is 4.8.0 or later, and Claude Code is 2.1.228 or later. The others can print any version. This guide was written with Claude Code 2.1.312 and now-sdk 4.13.6. command not found counts as missing.

                                                                                      Did every version pass?

                                                                                      If one is missing or too old: install each tool that failed, in the order below. Skip the ones that passed. Then run the checks again.

                                                                                      Node.js: download the macOS installer, the .pkg file, from https://nodejs.org/en/download. Then run it.

                                                                                      8. In a new Terminal window (Cmd+N), run node --version. It prints a version, such as v26.13.0.

On an ARM computer, pick the one ending in _windows_arm64.msi. If it isn't listed, first click the link that shows all the assets.

                                                                                      🛟 An install or a check doesn't work on Mac

                                                                                      • "command not found" just after installing: open a new Terminal window and check again. If claude is still not found, its folder isn't on your PATH yet. Your PATH is the list of folders your computer looks in for tools. In ⌨️ Terminal, run these two lines, then open a new window:

                                                                                        echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
                                                                                        1. echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrcAdds one line to the end of .zshrc, the settings file Terminal reads each time a window opens. That line tells Terminal to look for tools in .local/bin in your home folder too. Claude Code's installer puts claude there.
                                                                                        2. source ~/.zshrcReads that settings file again in this window, so it picks up the new line now. Every new window reads it by itself.

                                                                                      • EACCES or "permission denied" from npm: run the npm install line again with sudo in front. sudo runs a command as an administrator. Type your Mac's password. Nothing shows as you type. Then run sudo chown -R $(id -u):$(id -g) ~/.npm, so npm's cache stays yours. Never put sudo in front of the Claude Code line.

                                                                                      • No Open Anyway button for the GitHub CLI: your company manages your Mac. Tell your instructor before the day.

                                                                                      • An installer asks for an administrator's name and password: your company manages your Mac, so you can't install on it yourself. Tell your instructor before the day.

                                                                                      • claude --version still prints an old version after the installer: an earlier install of Claude Code is found first. Tell your instructor.

                                                                                      🛟 An install or a check doesn't work on Windows

                                                                                      • "command not found" or "is not recognized" just after installing: close every terminal window, then open a new one. A new tab isn't enough. If claude is still not found, its folder isn't on your PATH yet. Your PATH is the list of folders Windows searches for tools. In ⌨️ Terminal, in PowerShell, run these two lines, then open a new window:

                                                                                        $currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", 'User')
                                                                                        1. $currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')Reads your PATH, the list of folders Windows searches for tools. It keeps a copy as $currentPath for the next line. 'User' means your own list, not the one for every account on the computer.
                                                                                        2. [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", 'User')Saves your PATH again, with one folder added at the end. That's .local\bin in your user folder, where Claude Code's installer puts claude. Only windows you open after this see the change, so you open a new one.

                                                                                      • irm: command not found: you're in Git Bash. Open PowerShell, as above, and paste the line again.

                                                                                      • Git Bash isn't in Windows Terminal's Default profile list: run Git for Windows' installer again. On Select Components, tick Add a Git Bash Profile to Windows Terminal. If you have no Windows Terminal at all, on Windows 10, install it from the Microsoft Store first.

                                                                                      • Windows asks for an administrator's password, or won't install: your company manages your computer, so you can't install on it yourself. Tell your instructor before the day.

                                                                                      • EPERM or EBUSY from npm: close every other terminal window and VS Code. Then run the npm install line again.

                                                                                      • claude --version still prints an old version after the installer: an earlier install of Claude Code is found first. Tell your instructor.

                                                                                      🛟 It says "certificate", "fetch failed" or times out

                                                                                      It's your company's network. Tell your instructor before the day.

                                                                                      4. Sign in to GitHub and get this guide

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      You sign in once with gh. After that, git uses the same sign-in each time it clones or pushes. Cloning copies a repo from GitHub to your computer, and pushing sends your commits back. The guide you download holds files you run or read later. These are the lab's settings script and the customer's inputs.

                                                                                      The lab needs GitHub. Your company's GitLab can't stand in for it.

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why not GitLab?
                                                                                      • This guide is a private GitHub repo that you're invited to.
                                                                                      • gh, the GitHub CLI, signs you in and makes your app's repo. It works only with GitHub.
                                                                                      • The kit files your stories, milestones and pull requests on GitHub, through gh.
                                                                                      • Claude Code installs the kit from GitHub.

                                                                                      Nothing you build in the lab goes to your company's GitLab.

                                                                                      Do you have a GitHub account you can use for the lab?

                                                                                      If you have no account yet: make one. It's free and takes about 5 minutes.

                                                                                      1. 🌐 Browser: open https://github.com/signup.
                                                                                      2. Enter an email address you can read now, a password and a user name. Any user name works. Your instructor uses it to invite you.
                                                                                      3. Type the code GitHub emails you, and follow the screens.
                                                                                      4. Send your instructor your user name. Their invite comes by email.

                                                                                      ✅ https://github.com/<your user name> shows your profile. Made it?

                                                                                      5. Add the lab's Claude Code settings

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      These settings fence Claude in for the lab. Claude starts in auto mode. In auto mode, it asks you less and blocks risky commands by itself. It still asks before any SDK command that writes to your instance. The settings block now-sdk auth. They turn off connectors, which link Claude to other apps, new memories and web search. They also keep Claude out of your notes, this guide and your keys, the files that hold your passwords and tokens. Any settings you had are backed up first, and Module 8 puts them back.

                                                                                      Have you used Claude Code on this computer before?

                                                                                      If you have: close every other Claude Code window first. Type /exit in each terminal, and close each session in the desktop app.

                                                                                      The lab's settings change how Claude works:

                                                                                      • Claude starts in auto mode.
                                                                                      • Connectors, new memories and web search are off.
                                                                                      • now-sdk auth is blocked.
                                                                                      • Claude asks you before the SDK commands that write to your instance, such as now-sdk install.
                                                                                      • Claude stays out of your notes, this guide and your keys: ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, gh's login, ~/.npmrc and ~/.netrc.

                                                                                      Your own settings are backed up and kept. Your own auto mode rules wait in the backup. Module 8 restores them. Cleanest of all is a separate user account on your computer.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal:

                                                                                      node ~/projects/hr-case-router-lab-guide/files/merge-claude-settings.mjs

                                                                                      ✅ It prints Lab settings in place.

                                                                                      7. Connect the SDK to your instance

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      The SDK needs a saved sign-in to read your instance and install your app on it. Every SDK command in the lab uses that sign-in by its name, lab-pdi. You type the password yourself. Claude is never allowed to run now-sdk auth, so it never sees your password.

                                                                                      Your instance must be awake. Type the password only here, never in Claude.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal: replace dev123456 with your instance's name, from its address in step 1. It's already done if the name is in Your values, under Setup, the first button in the top bar:

                                                                                      now-sdk auth --add https://dev123456.service-now.com --type basic --alias lab-pdi
now-sdk auth --list
                                                                                      1. now-sdk auth --add https://dev123456.service-now.com --type basic --alias lab-pdiSaves a sign-in to your instance on your computer, under the name lab-pdi. Every now-sdk command in the lab uses that name. basic means it signs in with a user name and password, which it asks you for.
                                                                                      2. now-sdk auth --listLists the sign-ins the SDK has saved. You can see lab-pdi is there, with your instance's address and the user name.

                                                                                      When asked, type the user name admin, then your admin password. Nothing shows while you type it.

                                                                                      ✅ The list shows [lab-pdi], then host = with your instance's address, and username = admin.

                                                                                      🛟 It prints a line starting [now-sdk] ERROR:

                                                                                      The sign-in failed. Check that the instance is awake and the password is right. Then run the first line again. If it says "certificate" or "fetch failed", or times out, that's your company's network. Tell your instructor.

                                                                                      Part 3 — The kit and a clean bench

                                                                                      8. Install the kit and the SDK plugin

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      The kit, prove-it, gives Claude the lab's stages: consult, design challenge, build plan, grade and handoff. Each stage proves itself before the next one starts. The kit's version is pinned, so it matches what this guide shows. The SDK plugin lets Claude look up facts instead of guessing them.

                                                                                      You install two plugins, add-ons for Claude Code. The kit runs the lab's rituals, the set routines it follows, such as shipping a pull request. ServiceNow's SDK plugin teaches Claude the SDK from its docs, with now-sdk explain. It also reads records on your instance, with now-sdk query. It can't write to the instance.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal:

                                                                                      claude plugin marketplace add 'gapietro/prove-it-kit#v0.1.4'
claude plugin install prove-it@prove-it
claude plugin install servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-official
                                                                                      1. claude plugin marketplace add 'gapietro/prove-it-kit#v0.1.4'Adds the kit's GitHub repo as a plugin marketplace, a list of plugins Claude Code can install. It adds version v0.1.4, the part after #.
                                                                                      2. claude plugin install prove-it@prove-itInstalls the kit's plugin, prove-it, from the marketplace you just added. The name after @ is the marketplace's, and it's prove-it too. Claude Code then has the plugin in every folder.
                                                                                      3. claude plugin install servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-officialInstalls ServiceNow's SDK plugin from claude-plugins-official, Anthropic's own plugin marketplace. It teaches Claude to look things up in the SDK's docs and to read records on your instance. Those lookups never change anything.

                                                                                      ✅ None of the three prints an error.

                                                                                      🛟 It says the marketplace claude-plugins-official isn't known

                                                                                      Add it, then run the last line again:

                                                                                      claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official
claude plugin install servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-official
                                                                                      1. claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-officialAdds Anthropic's own plugin marketplace to Claude Code, from its GitHub repo. Most installs already have it. Yours didn't, so the SDK plugin's install couldn't find it.
                                                                                      2. claude plugin install servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-officialInstalls ServiceNow's SDK plugin from claude-plugins-official, Anthropic's own plugin marketplace. It teaches Claude to look things up in the SDK's docs and to read records on your instance. Those lookups never change anything.
                                                                                      🛟 It says "blocked by enterprise policy"

                                                                                      Your organisation limits plugins. Stop here, and tell your instructor what it says.

                                                                                      9. Make your folders

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      Your workspace keeps everything for your app in one place. The app's repo goes in it. In Module 1, the PRD goes in brief. The PRD is the product requirements document, which says what the app must do. Claude logs each catch in catches.md. With projects open in VS Code, you can read every file Claude writes.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal:

                                                                                      mkdir -p ~/projects/hr-case-router/brief
touch ~/projects/hr-case-router/catches.md
                                                                                      1. mkdir -p ~/projects/hr-case-router/briefMakes your workspace folder, hr-case-router inside projects, with a brief folder in it. You put the PRD in brief in Module 1. -p makes any folder that's missing on the way, and doesn't complain if they're already there.
                                                                                      2. touch ~/projects/hr-case-router/catches.mdMakes an empty file, catches.md, in your workspace. Claude logs each catch in it. If the file is already there, touch leaves what's in it alone.

                                                                                      hr-case-router is your workspace, the folder for everything about your app. Claude logs catches in catches.md.

                                                                                      ✏️ Editor: in VS Code, choose File > Open Folder… and open the projects folder in your home folder. Keep it open.

                                                                                      10. Check nothing else is loaded

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      Anything else Claude loads changes how it behaves and what it can do. That includes another plugin, an MCP server, a hook or your own instruction file. The lab's steps and checks expect only the kit and the SDK plugin. So anything extra goes off for now, and Module 8 brings it back.

                                                                                      Claude loads every plugin, MCP server, hook and instruction file you have. An MCP server connects Claude to another app or service. A hook is a command that runs by itself at set moments. For the lab, Claude should load only the kit and the SDK plugin.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal:

                                                                                      cd ~/projects/hr-case-router
claude plugin list
claude mcp list
ls -d ~/CLAUDE.md ~/projects/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/skills ~/.claude/agents ~/.claude/commands
grep -c '"hooks"' ~/.claude/settings.json
git config --get core.hooksPath
                                                                                      1. cd ~/projects/hr-case-routerGoes into your workspace, so the checks see what Claude sees when it starts there.
                                                                                      2. claude plugin listLists the plugins Claude Code has installed, and whether each is enabled. A plugin adds skills, commands or hooks to every session. So an extra one changes how Claude behaves in the lab.
                                                                                      3. claude mcp listLists the MCP servers Claude can use. These are tools outside Claude Code, such as a connection to another app or service.
                                                                                      4. ls -d ~/CLAUDE.md ~/projects/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/skills ~/.claude/agents ~/.claude/commandsLooks for your own instruction files and folders. These are a CLAUDE.md in your home folder, in projects or in ~/.claude, and your own skills, agents and commands. Claude reads them in every session. -d lists each one by name, not what's inside it, and No such file or directory means it isn't there, which is what you want.
                                                                                      5. grep -c '"hooks"' ~/.claude/settings.jsonCounts how often "hooks" appears in Claude Code's settings file. Hooks are commands Claude runs by itself at set moments. 0 means you have none.
                                                                                      6. git config --get core.hooksPathPrints the folder git takes its commit hooks from, if one is set for every repo on your computer. Nothing printed means each repo uses its own hooks. Then your repo's guard, which you set up in steps 13 and 14, will run.

                                                                                      ✅ The only enabled plugins are prove-it@prove-it, with Version: 0.1.4, and servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-official, at any version. claude mcp list says No MCP servers configured. ls prints only No such file or directory lines. grep prints 0, and git config prints nothing.

                                                                                      🛟 Other plugins or MCP servers are listed

                                                                                      ⌨️ First, save what you have, once. Module 8 uses it to switch them back on:

                                                                                      cd ~/projects/hr-case-router-notes
[ -e plugins-before-lab.txt ] || claude plugin list > plugins-before-lab.txt
[ -e mcp-before-lab.json ] || (umask 077; node -p 'JSON.stringify(require(require("os").homedir()+"/.claude.json").mcpServers||{},null,2)' > mcp-before-lab.json)
                                                                                      1. cd ~/projects/hr-case-router-notesGoes into your lab notes folder. The next two lines write their files there, where Module 8 looks for them.
                                                                                      2. [ -e plugins-before-lab.txt ] || claude plugin list > plugins-before-lab.txtSaves the list of your plugins, and which are enabled, in plugins-before-lab.txt. Module 8 uses it to know which to switch back on. [ -e … ] || means "only if that file isn't there yet", so a second run never overwrites your record.
                                                                                      3. [ -e mcp-before-lab.json ] || (umask 077; node -p 'JSON.stringify(require(require("os").homedir()+"/.claude.json").mcpServers||{},null,2)' > mcp-before-lab.json)Copies your MCP servers' settings out of ~/.claude.json, Claude Code's own file, into mcp-before-lab.json. Module 8 uses it to add them back after you remove them. umask 077 makes the new file readable only by you, because a server's settings can hold a key.

                                                                                      Then switch each one off by the name listed. For a plugin, run claude plugin disable <name>. For a server, run claude mcp remove <name>. A server whose name starts plugin: goes when you switch off its plugin. If one won't go, or you never added it, it's your organisation's. Leave it, and tell your instructor.

claude plugin marketplace add 'gapietro/prove-it-kit#v0.1.4'
claude plugin install prove-it@prove-it

                                                                                      2. claude plugin marketplace add 'gapietro/prove-it-kit#v0.1.4'Adds the kit's GitHub repo as a plugin marketplace, a list of plugins Claude Code can install. It adds version v0.1.4, the part after #.
                                                                                      3. claude plugin install prove-it@prove-itInstalls the kit's plugin, prove-it, from the marketplace you just added. The name after @ is the marketplace's, and it's prove-it too. Claude Code then has the plugin in every folder.

                                                                                      Your own setup would steer the lab. Add .off to the end of each name ls lists, such as mv ~/CLAUDE.md ~/CLAUDE.md.off. Module 8 moves them back. If grep or git config shows hooks, tell your instructor. A separate user account on your computer is cleanest.

                                                                                      Part 4 — Your app's repo

                                                                                      Your app's code gets its own repo, fenced in two ways. It ignores every file you haven't named. A guard checks each commit for secrets, such as passwords and tokens.

                                                                                      11. Look up your scope

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      Your scope is your app's own name space on the instance. Every table, property and role the app makes starts with it. The SDK needs it to create the app. The vendor prefix in it is the one your instance gives its own apps.

                                                                                      🌐 Browser:

                                                                                      1. As admin, type sys_properties.list in the filter navigator, the box under All, and press Enter. In the Name column's search box, type glide.appcreator.company.code and press Enter. Its Value is your vendor prefix, such as 123456.
                                                                                      2. Your scope is x_<prefix>_hcr_<your initials, lower case>, such as x_123456_hcr_ga.

                                                                                      ✅ Your scope is all lower case, with 18 characters or fewer.

                                                                                      Note your scope.

                                                                                      12. Create the app

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      now-sdk init makes your app's starting files: its project settings, its build setup and a src folder for the code. Everything Claude builds later goes on top of them. While it works, it reaches your instance through lab-pdi. That's why the instance must be awake.

                                                                                      Your instance must be awake.

                                                                                      ⌨️ Terminal: replace <SCOPE> with your scope from step 11. It's already done if you typed your scope in step 11:

                                                                                      mkdir -p ~/projects/hr-case-router/app
cd ~/projects/hr-case-router/app
now-sdk init --appName "HR Case Router" --packageName hr-case-router --scopeName <SCOPE> --template typescript.basic --auth lab-pdi
                                                                                      1. mkdir -p ~/projects/hr-case-router/appMakes the app folder inside your workspace. Your app's code lives there, and later its repo. -p doesn't complain if it's already there.
                                                                                      2. cd ~/projects/hr-case-router/appGoes into that folder, because now-sdk init makes the app in the folder you're in.
                                                                                      3. now-sdk init --appName "HR Case Router" --packageName hr-case-router --scopeName <SCOPE> --template typescript.basic --auth lab-pdiMakes the starting files of a new ServiceNow app in this folder, from the SDK's basic TypeScript template. TypeScript is the language the app's code is written in. It names the app HR Case Router, gives it your scope, and reaches your instance through the lab-pdi sign-in.

                                                                                      ✅ It ends with Application created successfully.

                                                                                      🛟 It fails, or you're not sure it worked

                                                                                      ⌨️ Run ls ~/projects/hr-case-router/app/now.config.json. If it's listed, the app exists, so go on. If it isn't, check your scope. It must be lower case, with 18 characters at most, and no < or >. Then run cd ~/projects/hr-case-router && rm -rf app, and the three lines above. If it still fails, tell your instructor.

                                                                                      13. Let Claude set up the repo

                                                                                      ℹ️ Why this step

                                                                                      Your app's folder becomes a repo, with its safety in place before anything is committed. The allow list, .gitignore, means git tracks only the files it names. The guard is a script git runs before each commit. It refuses a file the list doesn't name, or a line shaped like a secret. Your commits carry your GitHub noreply address, an address GitHub gives you so your own email stays private.

                                                                                      In the terminal: ⌨️ start Claude in the app folder. Pick Yes when it asks if you trust the folder:

                                                                                      cd ~/projects/hr-case-router/app && claude

                                                                                      In the Code tab: 🤖 start a new session (Cmd+N (Mac) · Ctrl+N (Windows)). In the row under the prompt box, pick the top entry under Local. Click the folder control, choose Open folder… and pick ~/projects/hr-case-router/app. Then press Ctrl+O until the view is Verbose.

                                                                                      🤖 Claude: paste this, type go after it, and press Enter:

                                                                                      Set up this folder as my app's repo. Make sure ~/projects/prove-it-kit is
gapietro/prove-it-kit at tag v0.1.4: clone it if it's missing, otherwise
fetch tags and switch to the tag. Run git init -b main. For this repo only,
