                                                                                      Getting it to production

                                                                                      Lab home · ← Your own PRD track · Labels in Claude's output →

                                                                                      ⏱ Set by your company's change calendar · book your platform team now

                                                                                      Everything in this lab runs on a development instance, on purpose. A development instance is for building apps, and nobody does real work on it. Your company also has a test instance, where apps are tried before they go live, and production, the instance real people use. Claude never touches test or production. Nothing in the kit does either. A finished app reaches production through your company's own change process. The people who own those instances run it.

                                                                                      The workshop app is a teaching copy. It's built on a lab instance, in the lab's scope, the app's own space on the platform. It can't be promoted as built. To take the HR Case Router to production, run it as your own PRD on your company's development instance. Build it with:

                                                                                      • your company's routing rules, article and restricted services, the HR services whose cases never go to the AI;
                                                                                      • the agent's caps, its limits on runs per hour and per day, as the owner sets them;
                                                                                      • masking, which hides personal data from the AI, confirmed with your platform team, the people who run your company's instances;
                                                                                      • the override rule from After the workshop. It records each time someone moves a case after the router has.

                                                                                      Your platform team decides how apps move between your instances. So this page is a checklist, not a script.

                                                                                      1. The bar before you ask

                                                                                      None of these can be waived.

                                                                                      • ☐ The slice is done. A slice is the part of your app you build first. OWN-PRD.md section 5 says when it's done.
                                                                                      • ☐ GRADE.md holds a HANDOFF grade of 75 or more. A preview doesn't count. Its Caps applied table is empty, so no failed check limits the score.
                                                                                      • ☐ HANDOFF.md says READY. NOT READY means someone else couldn't run the app from the runbook, the steps for running and fixing it. Nobody can accept that on paper.
                                                                                      • ☐ The real owner has seen it work live as an ordinary user. The real owner is the person in your company who owns the requirements. The DEMO stories are closed, and they record that the owner saw it.
                                                                                      • ☐ The app has an on switch. It's a setting that an admin controls, and it turns all the app's logic off. It's a term in the design, with a test. The runbook's Recovery section names it. Without it, the only way to stop the app is to back it all out, removing the whole app.

                                                                                      What can be accepted: an open story, but only for a check that doesn't cap the grade, such as code.lint or ready.config-documented. The real owner must accept it in writing. Record it in docs/PROMOTION.md, the file you start in section 2. Write who accepted it, when, and the date it will be closed. These checks cap the grade, so they're never accepted: code.build, code.tests, code.secrets, design.signed, design.terms-tested, design.gates-evidenced, code.oob, ready.ai-bounded and ready.install.

                                                                                      2. Agree how it moves

                                                                                      Meet your platform team before you raise anything. ✏️ Editor: write their answers in docs/PROMOTION.md, in your app's repo. docs/ is already admitted: the project's .gitignore lets git track it.

                                                                                      1. The delivery mechanism. This is how a scoped app, one that keeps to its own scope, moves from development to test to production in your company. Ask them rather than assume.
                                                                                      2. Who installs. On test and production, their team installs. Claude never does, and ideally the builder doesn't either.
                                                                                      3. Global and shared changes. These are anything the app changes outside its own scope, such as shared tables or global rules. Your LLD, the low-level design, lists them in §2–§3. They usually need their own approval.
                                                                                      4. Cross-scope access. This is the app reading or changing records that belong to another scope. On dev, the platform may record cross-scope access for you as the app runs. On test and production it may not, and logic that worked on dev fails. Make sure every cross-scope privilege the app needs is declared in source, written into the app's code. Your LLD §4 lists them. Confirm them with your platform team. One isn't the app's to declare. The lab setup made HR's two security-policy tables readable from other app scopes, so the access check can read them. Your instances need the same setting, made by their admin.
                                                                                      5. Demo data stays out of production. Your seed records, the demo records the app installs, are part of the app's source. So they'd install everywhere. Agree how they're left out of the production install. Then confirm that works on test.
                                                                                      ℹ️ What §2–§3 and §4 mean

                                                                                      § means section. In your LLD, §2 is its components, §3 its logic and §4 its security, with the access the app needs. All the labels.

                                                                                      6. **Per-instance configuration.** Some things differ on each instance: role-to-group assignments, settings, the agent's run-as user, and any integration's endpoint and credential. The run-as user is the account the agent works as. An admin sets each of them by hand, from the runbook. List them. 7. **Back-out.** This is how to remove the app if switching it off isn't enough, and what that costs. Uninstalling a scoped app may delete its tables and the data in them, such as log or audit rows. Confirm with your platform team. Write the agreed back-out in `docs/PROMOTION.md`. 8. **The AI agent**, if your app has one. Confirm these with your platform team, and record who confirmed them and when: - Its workflow, agent, tools and jobs are active, and each job has its trigger. - Its run-as user has only its own roles, never admin. Nothing else runs as it. - Masking covers what the tools return to the AI. Until that's confirmed, it blocks going to production. - The caps are the owner's values.

                                                                                      Then commit and ship it. 🤖 Claude, in ~/projects/<app>/app: Commit docs/PROMOTION.md on a new branch docs/promotion-agree. Then paste this, type go after it, and press Enter:

                                                                                      ship it. Review the diff without checking it out, and post the review's
findings on the pull request as a comment, even if there are none. Fix
real findings in the code once. Never edit docs/, GRADE.md, RUNBOOK.md,
HANDOFF.md or BACKLOG.md to answer a finding, and don't stop to ask me:
file it as a register issue instead. There's no CI: merge once now-sdk
build passes, and npm test too once there's a test script. Then switch to
main and pull, and give me the pull request link and one line per
finding: fixed, filed, or not a problem and why.

                                                                                      Claude pushes your branch and opens a pull request. It reviews its own diff without checking it out, and posts the review on the pull request. It fixes real findings once, files the rest, and merges when the build and tests pass. You get the pull request link and one line per finding.

                                                                                      🌐 Browser: ✅ the pull request link shows Merged. If Claude asks you something, or the pull request isn't merged, use the two 🛟 boxes under Module 7, step 7.

                                                                                      Then version, grade and tag it. That way test and production get exactly what was graded:

                                                                                      1. 🤖 Claude: paste this. Then ship it with the paste above:

                                                                                        Run npm version 1.0.0 --no-git-tag-version, so package.json and
package-lock.json say 1.0.0, never now.config.json. Commit both on a
new branch chore/version-1.0.0.

                                                                                        Claude sets the app's version to 1.0.0 in package.json and package-lock.json. It leaves now.config.json alone, and commits both files on a new branch. Once that's shipped, the grade and the tag that follow are of version 1.0.0.

                                                                                      2. Grade at HANDOFF again, on main as it is now. Follow After the workshop, Part 4, step 7, with these changes:

                                                                                        • type <alias> for the alias;
                                                                                        • type OWN-PRD section 7's register reply;
                                                                                        • use the branch chore/grade-v1.0.0 in place of chore/grade-handoff.

                                                                                        ✅ It still meets section 1's bar.

                                                                                      3. ⌨️ Terminal, in ~/projects/<app>/app: tag the commit that holds that GRADE.md. A tag is a fixed name for exactly that code. Then push the tag:

                                                                                        git switch main && git pull && git status --short
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Slice 1: <what a user can now do>"
git push origin v1.0.0
git diff --stat <the commit GRADE.md says it graded> v1.0.0
                                                                                        1. git switch main && git pull && git status --shortSwitches to main, downloads what's been merged into it on GitHub, then lists every file that's changed but not committed. && runs each command only if the one before it worked. Nothing listed means your folder holds exactly what's on main.
                                                                                        2. git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Slice 1: <what a user can now do>"Tags the newest commit on main, the one that holds the grade, as version v1.0.0. -a stores your message with the tag. Replace <what a user can now do> with what this slice lets a user do.
                                                                                        3. git push origin v1.0.0Sends the tag to GitHub. Test and production can then install exactly the code that was graded.
                                                                                        4. git diff --stat <the commit GRADE.md says it graded> v1.0.0Lists the files that differ between the commit the grade looked at and the tagged one. Only the grade's own files should differ. That shows the tagged code is the code that was graded.

                                                                                        ✅ Status prints nothing, and the diff lists only GRADE.md, .gitignore and BACKLOG.md.

                                                                                      Never move a pushed tag. If anything changes after this, such as a runbook fix found on test, give it the next version, 1.0.1. Then do these three steps again.

                                                                                      3. Test, with the runbook only

                                                                                      1. Your platform team installs the tag on test. They follow RUNBOOK.md and nothing else. Then they do the per-instance configuration from section 2, item 6. If they need to ask you anything, that's a gap in the runbook. Fix it through the build loop on development, as in Module 6. Then version, grade and tag it again, as at the end of section 2, and start this step again.
                                                                                      2. First contact with real data. Test usually holds copies of real records. Re-run your live check as ordinary users. Do the same with After the workshop Part 2's attacks on your central rule, the one rule that must never break. Check that the cross-scope access works here. If your app has an agent, run it on a copied real record. Then confirm with your platform team that what its tools returned was masked. Anything that fails goes back through the build loop on development. Never fix it on test.
                                                                                      3. Rehearse Recovery on test. Switch the app off with its on switch. Check that it really stops. Then switch it back on. If the platform team allows it, rehearse the agreed back-out too.
                                                                                      4. Re-run the handoff drill on test, if the platform team allows a planted failure there. A planted failure is a fault someone causes on purpose, for you to find from the runbook.

                                                                                      ✅ Check: every result is in docs/PROMOTION.md, with dates and who ran it. Nothing was fixed on test by hand. Commit and ship it as in section 2, on a new branch docs/promotion-test.

                                                                                      4. The change request

                                                                                      A change request is your company's formal request to change production. Raise it through your company's change process. Attach the evidence itself, not a summary of it:

                                                                                      Evidence From
                                                                                      What changes, and what doesn't The signed design record, and LLD §1
                                                                                      How well it's built GRADE.md in the tag, and the commit it graded
                                                                                      Whether someone else can run it HANDOFF.md and RUNBOOK.md
                                                                                      What was tested on test, and by whom docs/PROMOTION.md
                                                                                      How to switch it off, and how to back it out The runbook's Recovery section, and the back-out in docs/PROMOTION.md, rehearsed on test
                                                                                      Anything accepted rather than fixed docs/PROMOTION.md, with the owner's written acceptance

                                                                                      Say what isn't done. In the change request itself, list the capabilities that SLICE.md defers. Approvers should never discover a gap after go-live.

                                                                                      5. Production

                                                                                      1. Your platform team installs the same tag from the runbook, without the demo data. Then they do the per-instance configuration, including the agent's production caps.
                                                                                      2. The on switch starts off. The app is installed, but its logic doesn't run yet. For the HR Case Router, the override rule ships and passes first.
                                                                                      3. The owner switches it on, at an agreed time, with you available.
                                                                                      4. Watch the first day. Use the checks the runbook gives an on-call person, the one who answers when something goes wrong. Those are the platform's own screens and the app's own lists and logs.
                                                                                      5. If it misbehaves: switch it off first. Then diagnose the problem from the runbook. Back out only if switching it off isn't enough, and only as agreed in docs/PROMOTION.md.

                                                                                      ✅ Check: it's on in production. The first day's checks are clean and written in docs/PROMOTION.md. The owner has signed off in the change request. Commit and ship it as in section 2, on a new branch docs/promotion-live.

                                                                                      6. After go-live

                                                                                      • The next slice extends the same design. OWN-PRD.md section 6 shows how. It goes through the design challenge again before any code is written.
                                                                                      • Anything found in production becomes a story on the board. It's built through the loop on development, then promoted with this page again. Never fix it by hand in production.

                                                                                      Appendix — Labels in Claude's output

                                                                                      Lab home · ← Getting it to production

                                                                                      Claude, the kit and the lab's files name things with short labels. The kit is prove-it, the Claude Code plugin the lab runs on. Most labels are a letter and a number, such as C3, P8 or §7. This page says what each label means and where to look it up. Any step whose output uses a label also has an ℹ️ box that explains it right there.

                                                                                      C3 isn't capability 3. The PRD's capabilities have no letter. They're written out, as "capability 3". C3 is rule 3 of your design record, the design you confirm in Module 4. Claude may still call a capability C3 in the consult or the LLD. That's its own shorthand, so read it as capability 3 there. From Module 4 on, a C number is only ever a design term. Module 5 checks that your LLD uses none.

                                                                                      Label In plain words Where it's written You first meet it
                                                                                      capability 1 to 9 One of the nine things the PRD asks the app to do The PRD, section 3 Module 1
                                                                                      R2, R8… One of the customer's requirements inputs/USE-CASE.md Module 1, step 2
                                                                                      P1 to P15 A platform rule: something your instance really does that the build must allow for docs/DECISIONS.md, "Platform rules" Module 3, step 1
                                                                                      D1, D2… A question your LLD can't settle yet Your LLD, section 8 Module 3, step 4
                                                                                      C1, C2… A design term: one rule of your design record that a test or a person can check Your design record, section 3 Module 4, step 3
                                                                                      §1, §7… Section 1, section 7 of a document The design record or your LLD Module 3, step 4
                                                                                      M1 · merge… A milestone: the stories one gate needs GitHub, Milestones Module 5, step 2
                                                                                      p0, p1, p2 A story's priority: how soon its gate comes GitHub, Labels Module 5, step 2
                                                                                      design.terms-tested… One of the grade's checks GRADE.md Module 7, step 5

                                                                                      Capabilities 1 to 9, no letter

                                                                                      These are the nine things the PRD asks the app to do. They're listed in its section 3, "Capabilities requested". Claude writes them out, as "capability 3". Or it uses a bare number: in a table's # column, as in CONSULT.md, or in brackets, such as "the weekly numbers (9)". Capabilities 3 and 5 use AI. Capability 3 routes a new case. Capability 5 routes it again when a fulfiller, someone who works HR cases, clicks Reroute. Capability 4 is the checks on every move the agent wants to make.

                                                                                      R2, R8…: the customer's requirements

                                                                                      These are the customer's own numbers for their requirements. They're in the customer's use case, inputs/USE-CASE.md. Each requirement says how much it matters. Must is a must-have. Should is wanted but not essential. The numbers are the customer's, so some are missing. You meet them in Module 1. There Claude traces each line of the PRD back to the inputs, and quotes them.

                                                                                      P1 to P15: platform rules

                                                                                      These are things your ServiceNow instance really does that the build must allow for. They're in the "Platform rules" table of docs/DECISIONS.md, each with its reason. Each comes from a real failure, or from a new risk that AI agents bring. You'll meet two of them often:

                                                                                      • P7: every install turns off the router's on switch, the setting that lets its logic run. So you set it back to true after each install.
                                                                                      • P8: the first runs after an install may each fail once per HR table. Run again.

                                                                                      The lab's test file, src/platform-rules.test.ts, checks P1 to P5, P12 and P13 each time npm test runs. The live checks, run on your instance, prove the rest. An upper-case P is a platform rule. A lower-case p0 to p2 is a priority, explained below.

                                                                                      D1, D2…: open decisions in your LLD

                                                                                      These are the questions your LLD can't settle yet. The LLD is the low-level design: how each part of the app will be built. Its section 8 lists them. Claude never guesses an answer. Each one waits for the customer, or for Module 4's design challenge. The challenge either decides it or leaves it out of this release. D numbers belong to the LLD only. So they never clash with the design record's C numbers.

                                                                                      C1, C2…: design terms

                                                                                      These are the numbered rules of your design record, docs/DESIGN-HRCaseRouter.md, in its section 3. Think of C as contract. Once you confirm the record in Module 4, it's the contract the build follows. Each term is one rule in it that a test or a person can check, such as "only apply_route changes a case".

                                                                                      • A term keeps its number for good, even if it changes later. The change goes in the record's drift log, section 10.
                                                                                      • Each test's name starts with the number of the term it proves, such as C12: a run's target is its log row, never the case. A prompt writes this as C<n>. Claude puts the real number in its place.
                                                                                      • The grade counts a term as tested only when a test's name or file names its number.

                                                                                      §1, §7…: sections of a document

                                                                                      § means section. §7 is section 7 of the document the sentence is about. That's usually the design record, and sometimes your LLD.

                                                                                      § The design record Your LLD
                                                                                      §1 Summary: what's built, and why Scope: each capability, built or deferred
                                                                                      §2 Context: the documents it relies on Components: the parts of the app
                                                                                      §3 Terms: the numbered rules, C1, C2… Logic: what runs, and when
                                                                                      §4 Data: each table, and who may change it Security: roles and access
                                                                                      §5 Failures, and how each is handled Failures, one per component
                                                                                      §6 Security and access Test plan
                                                                                      §7 Gates: what each must pass Research log: the facts you checked
                                                                                      §8 The options turned down, and why Open decisions: D1, D2…
                                                                                      §9 Approval: who confirmed it, and when
                                                                                      §10 Drift log: every change after approval

                                                                                      M1 · merge…: milestones

                                                                                      The build plan files one GitHub milestone for each gate. They're numbered in the order you reach them, such as M1 · merge and M2 · install. A milestone holds the stories its gate needs. A gate passes only when its stories are done. The grade marks one milestone at a time. Module 7 grades the merge gate.

                                                                                      p0, p1, p2: priority labels

                                                                                      This is a story's priority on GitHub. It depends only on how soon the story's gate comes:

                                                                                      • p0: it holds up the next gate. Do these first.
                                                                                      • p1: it holds up the gate after that.
                                                                                      • p2: further out.

                                                                                      The plan adds other labels too:

                                                                                      • gate:merge and the like: the story's gate.
                                                                                      • size:s, size:m or size:l: how big the story is.
                                                                                      • epic: a group of stories.
                                                                                      • register: something to rule on or keep for later, with no gate.

                                                                                      design.terms-tested…: the grade's checks

                                                                                      Each row of GRADE.md is one check. Its name is the area it looks at, a dot, then what it checks. design.terms-tested checks that a test names every design term. ready.gate-clear checks that the gate's stories are all closed. code.lint looks for a lint script, which checks the code's style. This lab doesn't use one. A cap limits the whole score when one serious check fails.
